title: Katakana K-Row — カ キ ク ケ コ

points.name: カ
points.explanation: カ makes the same 'ka' sound as hiragana か. Visually, カ is composed of two strokes that together look like a 'katakana-ish' version of the Roman letter 'K' — a diagonal sweep down-right and another stroke hooking off it. Compare this to hiragana か, which has a more complex looping structure. One way to remember カ is to look for a knife shape — the strokes form a cutting blade. カ appears in カメラ (camera), カード (card), and カフェ (café), making it immediately useful for recognizing Japan's abundant café culture vocabulary.
rules: Same unaspirated 'ka' as か — no puff of air after the consonant.
カ looks like a simplified 'K' — two strokes forming a sharp angular shape.
Memory trick: カ looks like a katakana 'K' for 'ka'.

points.name: キ
points.explanation: キ makes the same 'ki' sound as hiragana き. Visually, キ has three horizontal strokes crossed by a vertical stroke — it looks like a 'key' (three lines crossed by one shaft), which is a convenient memory hook since キ sounds like 'key'! Compare this to hiragana き, which has a more cursive structure. キ appears in キッチン (kitchen), キャンプ (camp), and キーボード (keyboard). The extended dash ー in キーボード elongates the 'i' vowel — so キー is 'kii' (two beats).
rules: Same unaspirated 'ki' as き — bright 'ee' vowel after the 'k'.
キ has three horizontal strokes crossed by a vertical — looks like a 'key'. Memory hook!
Small キャ (ki + ya) creates the combination 'kya' — you'll see this in キャンプ (camp).
points.flashcardAnswer: ki — same sound as き; the character looks like a key

points.name: ク
points.explanation: ク makes the same 'ku' sound as hiragana く (with the flat, unrounded Japanese 'u'). Visually, ク has two strokes: a diagonal going down-right, and then a sweeping stroke hooking under and to the right — it looks a bit like a check mark or a swooping bird's beak. Compare to hiragana く, which is a single curved stroke. ク appears in クラス (class), クリスマス (Christmas), and クーラー (cooler / air conditioning unit). In everyday Japanese life, クーラー is often preferred over エアコン, so both words are useful.
rules: Same 'ku' as く — 'k' with flat, unrounded Japanese 'u'.
ク has two strokes, forming a kind of angular bird-beak or check-mark shape.
ク vs ワ: ク has a sweeping bottom-right hook; ワ curves back to the left.

points.name: ケ
points.explanation: ケ makes the same 'ke' sound as hiragana け. Visually, ケ looks quite similar to カ — both have a diagonal sweep and another stroke going right — but ケ has an additional horizontal stroke across the top. Think of ケ as カ with a hat. Alternatively, ケ resembles a katakana 'K' with an extra arm. ケ appears in ケーキ (cake), ケース (case), and ケータイ (mobile phone — a shortening of 'keitai denwa', 'portable telephone'). ケータイ is an interesting example of Japanese creating new words from loanword elements.
rules: Same 'ke' as け — unaspirated 'k' + pure 'eh' vowel.
ケ looks like カ with an extra horizontal stroke at the top — 'ケ = カ + hat'.
ケータイ (mobile phone) is a Japanese-coined abbreviation of keitai denwa (携帯[けいたい]電話[でんわ]).

points.name: コ
points.explanation: コ makes the same 'ko' sound as hiragana こ. Visually, コ is one of the simplest and most distinctive katakana characters — it looks exactly like the Roman letter 'C' or a backwards 'C' (opening to the right), made of two strokes. This is one of those katakana characters that many learners find the easiest to remember because of its geometric clarity. コ appears in essential everyday vocabulary: コーヒー (coffee), コンビニ (convenience store), コンサート (concert), and コンピューター (computer).
rules: コ looks like a backwards 'C' or a squared bracket shape — two strokes, very clean.
コンビニ (convenience store) is one of Japan's most beloved institutions — you'll use this word constantly.
points.flashcardAnswer: ko — same sound as こ; the character looks like a backwards 'C'

chapterPractice.prompt: What sound does this katakana make?
chapterPractice.explanation: コ makes the 'ko' sound — same as hiragana こ. It looks like a backwards 'C' or a squared bracket. コ appears in コーヒー (coffee) and コンビニ (convenience store).
キ and き make the same 'ki' sound. Katakana キ looks like three horizontal lines crossed by a vertical — like a 'key' — while hiragana き has a more flowing, cursive structure.

chapterPractice.prompt: What does this katakana word mean?
chapterPractice.explanation: コーヒー (koohii) means 'coffee'. コ (ko) + ー (long 'o') + ヒ (hi) + ー (long 'i') = 'koohii'. The ー marks extend the preceding vowel. Coffee is hugely popular in Japan!

chapterPractice.prompt: What does this katakana word mean?
chapterPractice.explanation: カメラ (kamera) means 'camera'. カ (ka) + メ (me) + ラ (ra) = kamera. Many loanwords shift slightly in pronunciation to fit Japanese phonology — 'camera' becomes 'kamera'.
